sources.title: Language History: Alutiit’stun—Like an Alutiiq
sources.annotation: Museum account connects early Alutiiq writing, multilingual life, English-only schooling and Elder-led learning. Its undated current speaker totals and class schedules are not adopted. This is a Kodiak-focused introduction, not a survey of every Sugpiaq region.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual HTML Written Alutiiq, New Languages, Schools, Reawakening and Elder Teachers sections read. Images and recordings not reused or played; spiritual symbolism, archaeological locations and unverified current figures excluded.

sources.title: Alutiiq / Sugpiaq: language and dialect introduction
sources.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks
sources.annotation: Short university orientation distinguishes Koniag and Chugach dialect geography and points to literacy scholarship. Retained as supporting context; its undated population and speaker figures are not presented as current. Linked grammars and dictionaries require separate review.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual naming, dialect and literacy paragraphs read; no linked publication or audio reviewed. Short supporting introduction, outside substantive target.

sections.title: Literacy, schooling and Elder teachers
sections.text: The museum describes Alutiiq men developing early written records using Cyrillic and translating religious texts. Russian, Slavonic, Alutiiq and later English had different roles in community life. Its account also explains English-only schooling and the pressure it placed on family language transmission. Elder teachers subsequently contributed recordings, mentoring and new terms. This is a history of institutions and people making choices under changing conditions, without adopting the page’s undated speaker totals.

sections.title: A community plan for language learning
sections.text: The Qik Committee approved its2024–2029 plan for the Kodiak region in August2024. It seeks stronger links with village and off-island learners, progression toward fluency, teacher preparation and sustainable resources. It also proposes a shared base for language learning. These goals show how the community organizes future work; proposed speaker numbers, funding arrangements and institutional changes must not be mistaken for demonstrated results.

sections.title: How the teaching lessons build words
sections.text: The museum’s lessons explain that Alutiiq words combine stems with meaningful endings. Their noun examples distinguish one, two and three-or-more, while other endings can express relationships or change a word’s function. The teaching account cautions that a dictionary’s separate entries cannot simply be strung together as English words might be. The lessons are useful introductions to patterns; learning to speak also involves people and practice.

sections.title: Regional language context
sections.text: The university introduction distinguishes Koniag and Chugach dialect geography across Kodiak, the Alaska Peninsula, Kenai and Prince William Sound. This helps place the Kodiak-centered museum materials within a wider Sugpiaq setting. It is a short orientation, rather than fresh evidence of current speakers, and does not make every regional community or government interchangeable.
